TOXICOLOGY__Paracetamol Level & Nomogram:
The paracetamol treatment nomogram is a timed plasma-level tool used after acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose — the commonest deliberate self-poisoning in the UK — to decide who needs the antidote N-acetylcysteine (NAC). A single blood level taken at a known time is plotted against a graph of concentration versus hours since ingestion; falling on or above the treatment line identifies patients at risk of hepatotoxicity who must be treated.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Paracetamol is normally conjugated (glucuronidation/sulfation) and safely excreted. In overdose these pathways saturate and excess drug is oxidised by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI. NAPQI is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione; once glutathione stores are depleted, free NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins causing centrilobular (zone 3) hepatic necrosis, and can also cause acute kidney injury.

NAC replenishes glutathione, allowing NAPQI to be safely mopped up — it is most effective the earlier it is given.
Ingestion of ≥150 mg/kg (or ≥12 g total) confers significant risk of hepatotoxicity.
2SAMPLING & TIMING

For a single acute overdose with a known time, take the plasma paracetamol level at 4 hours post-ingestion or later. Absorption is incomplete before 4 hours, so earlier levels are uninterpretable and must never be used to exclude toxicity.

Also check salicylate level, U&Es, LFTs, INR/PT, venous bicarbonate and venous blood gas / lactate in any overdose.
Plot the single level on the nomogram against time since ingestion — the UK uses a single treatment line at 100 mg/L at 4 hours (the "100 line").
3INTERPRETATION
Level ON or ABOVE the treatment line→Start NAC — at risk of hepatotoxicity
Staggered overdose or uncertain timing of ingestion→Treat with NAC regardless of level (nomogram not valid)
Presentation >8 h after ingestion→Start NAC immediately; do NOT wait for the level
Ingestion ≥150 mg/kg→Significant risk — treat
Level below the line, <4 h sample→Uninterpretable — repeat at 4 h or later
4PROGNOSIS & PITFALLS

Deterioration to acute liver failure is assessed for transplant using the King's College Criteria. Watch for late presentation, malnutrition/enzyme-inducing states, and reliance on early levels.

🧪Arterial pH <7.3
After resuscitation — single criterion for transplant referral
🩸INR >6.5 / PT >100 s
Part of the triad (all three together)
💧Creatinine >300 µmol/L
Part of the triad
🧠Grade III/IV encephalopathy
Part of the triad — transplant if all three present
🚩 Start NAC empirically WITHOUT waiting for the level if presentation is delayed >8 h, the overdose is staggered, or the timing is unknown. A paracetamol level taken before 4 hours cannot be plotted and must NOT be used to exclude toxicity.
🎓 UK nomogram = a single treatment line at 100 mg/L at 4 h. NAC is most effective within 8 h of ingestion. Always check paracetamol AND salicylate levels in any unknown or mixed overdose.
TOXICOLOGY__Salicylate Level:
The salicylate (aspirin) level is a timed serum measurement used to confirm and quantify salicylate poisoning and guide escalation of treatment. Salicylate is a metabolic poison: it first stimulates the brainstem respiratory centre (causing a respiratory alkalosis) and then uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, generating lactate and organic acids that produce a raised anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The classic fingerprint is therefore a MIXED respiratory alkalosis plus metabolic acidosis. Because absorption is prolonged and erratic, a single early level can seriously underestimate the true burden.

1Indication & principle

Request a salicylate level in any suspected aspirin overdose or in an unexplained mixed acid-base disturbance with tinnitus, hyperventilation and sweating. The toxicodynamics are stepwise:

Central stimulation: salicylate directly stimulates the medullary respiratory centre → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis (earliest, often dominant in adults).
Metabolic poisoning: uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, impaired Krebs cycle and lipolysis → lactate, ketoacids and salicylic acid accumulate → raised anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
The combination gives the characteristic mixed picture; children and late/severe presentations tip towards a dominant acidosis.
🧪Salicylate level
Confirms and quantifies exposure; repeated to track absorption.
🫁ABG
Reveals the mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis and degree of acidaemia.
🧂U&E + K⁺
Hypokalaemia is common and blocks effective urinary alkalinisation.
🍬Glucose
Neuroglycopenia can occur with normal serum glucose; keep it in the normal-high range.
2How it is performed & sampling

Take a venous serum salicylate level, ideally at least 2 hours after ingestion in a symptomatic patient (or 4 hours from a known time), together with an ABG, U&E, glucose and paracetamol level. The single most important sampling rule is to REPEAT the level because absorption is slow and unpredictable, especially with enteric-coated or modified-release tablets or when a large bezoar of tablets forms.

Early tinnitus, nausea, hyperventilation, sweating→Clinical salicylate toxicity — send a level even before results of severity
Enteric-coated / staggered ingestion→Repeat levels every 2–3 h until falling — a single early level can rise further
Rising level on repeat sampling→Ongoing absorption — do not stand down; consider activated charcoal if within 1 h / large dose
3Interpretation & cut-offs

Interpret the number alongside the clinical picture and pH — a “moderate” level with acidaemia is more dangerous than a higher level with preserved compensation, because acidaemia drives salicylate into the CNS.

< 300 mg/L (< 2.2 mmol/L)→Usually asymptomatic / therapeutic range
≥ 500 mg/L (≥ 3.6 mmol/L) in adults→Significant toxicity — start IV fluids & urinary alkalinisation
ABG: low CO₂ + high anion-gap acidosis→Classic mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis
> 700 mg/L (> 5.1 mmol/L), acidaemia, CNS depression, seizures, renal failure or pulmonary oedema→Severe toxicity — refer for HAEMODIALYSIS

Treatment: give IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine (target urine pH 7.5–8.5). Ion-trapping keeps salicylate ionised in the tubular lumen and markedly enhances renal excretion. You must correct hypokalaemia first — the kidney cannot excrete an alkaline urine while it is avidly reabsorbing K⁺ in exchange for H⁺.

4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Falsely reassuring early level: the biggest trap — absorption continues, so a low first level does not exclude serious poisoning.
Acidaemia shifts salicylate into brain: a falling pH is an ominous sign even if the number is not extreme.
Failed alkalinisation: almost always due to uncorrected hypokalaemia.
Chronic toxicity: in elderly patients levels may be only modestly raised yet clinically severe — treat the patient, not the number.
🚩 Do NOT sedate, intubate and ventilate a salicylate-poisoned patient without expert (ICU/toxicology) input. These patients depend on their compensatory hyperventilation to defend blood pH; abolishing it causes catastrophic acidaemia, a surge of salicylate into the CNS and cardiac arrest. Severe toxicity, significant acidosis or a very high level warrant urgent haemodialysis.
🎓 The exam fingerprint is a MIXED respiratory alkalosis + raised anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Alkalinise the urine with IV sodium bicarbonate (correct K⁺ first), REPEAT the level as absorption continues, and dialyse the severe/acidaemic/high-level patient.
TOXICOLOGY__Carboxyhaemoglobin (CO Poiso:
Carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) measurement is a co-oximetry blood test used to confirm carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning — a diagnosis that is easy to miss because symptoms are non-specific and a standard pulse oximeter reads falsely normal. It quantifies the proportion of haemoglobin bound to CO, guiding oxygen therapy and the decision to escalate to hyperbaric treatment.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Suspect CO poisoning with faulty boilers/heaters, house fires, smoke inhalation, or deliberate self-harm (car exhaust in an enclosed space). Symptoms are non-specific: headache, nausea, dizziness and confusion — a key clue is multiple household members or pets affected together, or symptoms that improve away from the home.

CO binds haemoglobin with roughly 250× the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and displacing O₂.
It also shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, impairing offloading of the remaining oxygen to tissues.
Result: profound tissue hypoxia despite a normal PaO₂ (dissolved oxygen is unaffected).
2HOW IT IS MEASURED

%COHb is measured directly by CO-oximetry on a blood gas sample. Either a venous or arterial sample is acceptable — venous and arterial COHb correlate closely, so a venous sample avoids an unnecessary arterial puncture.

🚩 A standard pulse oximeter is falsely normal in CO poisoning — it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it over-reads SpO₂. A normal pulse oximetry reading AND a normal PaO₂ do NOT exclude CO poisoning: you must measure COHb directly.
3INTERPRETATION
Normal SpO₂ on pulse oximeter but hypoxic symptoms→Pulse oximetry unreliable — use CO-oximetry to measure %COHb
COHb >10% (non-smoker) or >15% (smoker)→Significant CO exposure confirmed
Raised COHb + headache/confusion→Give high-flow 100% oxygen via non-rebreathe mask
Syncope, seizures, cardiac ischaemia, pregnancy, very high COHb→Discuss hyperbaric oxygen therapy
🩸%COHb
Direct co-oximetry marker of CO burden
📈O₂ curve shift
Left shift — impaired tissue offloading
🧪PaO₂
Normal — falsely reassuring, does not exclude
🫀Lactate/ECG
Metabolic acidosis & ischaemia mark severity
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
%COHb correlates poorly with clinical severity — treat the patient and their symptoms, not just the number.
Levels fall once the patient is removed from the source and given oxygen, so a delayed sample may under-estimate exposure.
Smokers have a raised baseline (up to ~10%); interpret cut-offs accordingly.
Delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae can occur days to weeks later even after apparent recovery.
🚩 Give 100% high-flow oxygen immediately — do not wait for the COHb result. Oxygen shortens the COHb half-life from ~4–6 hours (on room air) to roughly ~90 minutes, and to ~20–30 minutes with hyperbaric oxygen.
🎓 Cherry-red skin is a late and rare sign — do not rely on it. The exam trap is the falsely reassuring pulse oximeter: SpO₂ and PaO₂ both look normal. Confirm with %COHb, treat everyone with high-flow 100% O₂, and reserve hyperbaric oxygen for severe features (loss of consciousness, neurology, cardiac ischaemia) or pregnancy.
TOXICOLOGY__Osmolar & Anion Gap (Toxic A:
The osmolar gap and anion gap are two bedside biochemical calculations used together to unmask poisoning by the toxic alcohols — methanol and ethylene glycol (antifreeze). They are the key to identifying an unexplained high anion gap metabolic acidosis with altered consciousness, where prompt recognition and antidote therapy prevent blindness, renal failure and death.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Suspect toxic alcohol poisoning in any patient with unexplained high anion gap metabolic acidosis and altered consciousness, or a history of ingesting antifreeze, screenwash, solvents or industrial spirits (including deliberate self-harm and chronic alcohol misusers seeking a substitute).

The pathophysiology is time-dependent, which is why two gaps are needed:

The parent alcohols are small, osmotically active molecules. Early after ingestion they raise the osmolar gap before any acidosis appears.
They are then metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) to toxic acids: methanol → formic acid; ethylene glycol → glycolic and oxalic acid. These raise the anion gap later.
🧪Osmolar gap
Measured osmolality − calculated osmolarity; raised by unmetabolised parent alcohol (early)
⚗️Anion gap
Na&splus; − (Cl− + HCO₃−); raised by accumulating acid metabolites (late)
🥃Methanol
→ formic acid: toxic to the optic nerve (visual loss)
❄️Ethylene glycol
→ glycolic/oxalic acid: calcium oxalate crystals, AKI, hypocalcaemia
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Both gaps are derived from routine venous bloods; no dynamic protocol is required, but interpretation depends on timing since ingestion.

Calculated osmolarity = 2 × Na&splus; + urea + glucose (all in mmol/L). Send a paired sample for measured osmolality by freezing-point depression osmometry.
Osmolar gap = measured osmolality − calculated osmolarity. A normal gap is roughly −10 to +10.
Anion gap = Na&splus; − (Cl− + HCO₃−); normal ≈ 8–16 mmol/L. Interpret alongside an arterial/venous blood gas showing the metabolic acidosis.
Supportive tests: serum methanol/ethylene glycol levels (often delayed in the UK — do not wait for them), urinary oxalate crystals, serum calcium, U&E and lactate. Some ethylene glycol antifreeze contains fluorescein, giving urine that fluoresces under Wood’s lamp.
3INTERPRETATION

Read the two gaps as a sequence in time, then use the end-organ clues to distinguish the two poisons.

Osmolar gap >10–15 (early, acidosis mild/absent)→Unmetabolised parent alcohol present — act now to block metabolism
High anion gap metabolic acidosis developing later→Toxic acid metabolites accumulating (formic / glycolic / oxalic acid)
Visual disturbance / “snow-field” vision, hyperaemic optic disc→Methanol — formic acid injuring the optic nerve; may cause permanent blindness
Calcium oxalate crystalluria, hypocalcaemia, rising creatinine→Ethylene glycol — oxalate deposition causing acute kidney injury
🎓 Osmolar gap EARLY, anion gap LATE. Methanol blinds (formic acid on the optic nerve); ethylene glycol crystallises (oxalate → renal failure and hypocalcaemia). The antidote for both is fomepizole.
4PITFALLS, SAFETY & TREATMENT

The commonest error is falsely reassuring oneself with a “normal” gap. The gaps evolve in opposite directions over time, so a single value can mislead.

A normal osmolar gap does NOT exclude poisoning in a late presentation — the parent alcohol may already be fully metabolised, leaving only a high anion gap.
Ethanol co-ingestion, ketoacidosis, renal failure and lactic acidosis all raise the osmolar or anion gap and can confound interpretation.
Treatment: fomepizole (first line) or ethanol competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, halting formation of the toxic acids. Add haemodialysis for severe acidosis, high measured levels, visual symptoms or end-organ damage — it removes both parent alcohol and metabolites. Give folinic acid (methanol) and a thiamine/pyridoxine cofactor (ethylene glycol) as adjuncts.
🚩 A normal osmolar gap does NOT rule out toxic alcohol poisoning if the patient presents late — by then the parent alcohol is metabolised and the danger shows only as a high anion gap acidosis. If the clinical suspicion is real, give fomepizole EARLY to block further metabolism and arrange urgent haemodialysis; do not wait for confirmatory alcohol levels.
TOXICOLOGY__Blood Gas & Lactate (Overdos:
The arterial or venous blood gas plus a lactate is the single fastest bedside investigation in the poisoned patient. It cannot name the toxin, but the acid–base pattern and the lactate together form a diagnostic fingerprint that triages severity in minutes and steers empirical antidotes long before the toxicology screen returns.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Order a VBG (or ABG if oxygenation/ventilation is in doubt) plus lactate in any significant overdose, reduced GCS, or unexplained collapse. A VBG gives pH, bicarbonate and lactate reliably and is quicker and less painful; use an ABG when you need an accurate PaO₂/PaCO₂ (respiratory failure, CO poisoning, salicylate).

The acid–base pattern reflects the mechanism of toxicity — unmeasured acids, hyperventilation, or hypoventilation.
Lactate reflects the balance of anaerobic production (cellular hypoxia, seizures, shock) versus reduced clearance (hepatic/renal failure).
Together they narrow a huge differential to a short, actionable list.

The key derived value is the anion gap = (Na⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normal ≈ 8–12 mmol/L. An unmeasured acid raises it.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Sample as early as possible — the initial gas is a severity baseline for trending.
Send paired U&Es from the same time point so the anion gap is calculated on matched electrolytes.
Add a paracetamol and salicylate level, glucose, and (where relevant) a co-oximetry sample for carboxyhaemoglobin — a standard SpO₂ probe cannot detect CO.
Repeat the gas and lactate to track the response to resuscitation and antidotes; a falling lactate is a marker of successful treatment.
3INTERPRETATION — THE FINGERPRINTS
High anion gap metabolic acidosis→toxic causes (MUDPILES-CAT): Methanol, Uraemia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylate, Cyanide, Alcohols, Toluene/CO
Mixed respiratory alkalosis + high anion gap metabolic acidosis→salicylate (aspirin) poisoning until proven otherwise
Very high lactate + profound acidosis with normal/high SpO₂ & PaO₂→cyanide or carbon monoxide — impaired cellular oxygen use, not delivery
High anion gap lactic acidosis + metformin use / AKI→metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA)
Respiratory acidosis (high PaCO₂) + low GCS→opioid or sedative overdose causing hypoventilation — consider naloxone
Raised lactate, otherwise unexplained→seizures, shock/hypoperfusion, or β-agonist (salbutamol/theophylline) toxicity
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
🩸Normal SpO₂ misleads
Pulse oximetry reads normal in CO and cyanide poisoning — oxygen delivery is fine, utilisation is not
🧪Salicylate evolves
Early respiratory alkalosis alone; the metabolic acidosis appears later — a single early gas can reassure falsely
⏱️Trend, don't snapshot
One value cannot grade a moving overdose; repeat to catch deterioration and confirm response
🧮Osmolar gap
Toxic alcohols may show a normal anion gap early but a raised osmolar gap before acid metabolites form
🚩 A rising lactate with a high anion gap acidosis despite adequate oxygenation should prompt urgent consideration of cyanide (smoke inhalation, industrial exposure) — give hydroxocobalamin empirically rather than waiting for confirmation. Profound metformin-associated lactic acidosis (pH < 7.1, lactate often > 15 mmol/L) is an indication for urgent haemodialysis.
🎓 Compute the anion gap on every serious overdose. Mixed respiratory alkalosis + high anion gap metabolic acidosis = salicylate. High lactate + severe acidosis + good SpO₂ = cellular hypoxia (CO or cyanide). A falling lactate is your best real-time sign that treatment is working.
TOXICOLOGY__TOXBASE / NPIS Guidance:
TOXBASE and the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) together form the UK poisons information system. TOXBASE is the online clinical toxicology database (the primary UK resource for managing poisoning), and the NPIS telephone line provides specialist advice for severe, complex, or unusual cases. This subtab is about a clinical decision pathway rather than a bedside assay: it tells you where to look and whom to call so that overdose management is evidence-based, agent-specific, and safe.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Use the poisons information system for ANY poisoning or overdose where management is uncertain — unfamiliar agent, uncertain dose, mixed ingestion, or an unexpected clinical course. The principle is evidence-based, agent-specific management driven by a structured risk assessment rather than guesswork.

TOXBASE — online database, free to registered UK clinical units, giving agent-specific risk assessment and management.
NPIS — 24-hour telephone line staffed by specialists in poisons for complex or severe cases.
Any overdose/exposure of uncertain management→Consult TOXBASE first
Severe, complex, or unusual poisoning→Telephone NPIS for specialist advice
2HOW IT IS USED — RISK ASSESSMENT

The core of every consultation is a structured risk assessment. Gather the key variables before searching TOXBASE, then follow the agent-specific entry through decontamination, antidotes, monitoring, and disposal.

Risk assessment→Agent, dose (mg/kg), timing since ingestion, comorbidity
Agent — exact drug/substance and formulation (modified-release changes timing).
Dose — estimate in mg/kg; compare against the toxic threshold on TOXBASE.
Timing — time since ingestion determines charcoal window and when to take timed levels (e.g. paracetamol at 4h).
Patient factors — weight, comorbidity, staggered vs single ingestion, co-ingestants.
3DECONTAMINATION & ANTIDOTES

Gut decontamination is selective, not routine. Activated charcoal adsorbs many drugs but only if given early and the airway is safe.

Activated charcoal decision→Generally within 1 hour of a significant ingestion if airway safe (NOT for alcohols, metals, lithium, hydrocarbons)

Know the high-yield antidote–toxin pairs:

💊Naloxone
Opioid toxicity
🧪N-acetylcysteine
Paracetamol overdose
⚠️Flumazenil
Benzodiazepines — rarely used, seizure risk
❤️DigiFab
Digoxin toxicity
🍸Fomepizole
Toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol)
💠Hydroxocobalamin
Cyanide poisoning
🧈IV lipid emulsion
Local anaesthetic / lipophilic-drug cardiotoxicity
🩸High-dose insulin-dextrose
Beta-blocker / calcium-channel-blocker toxicity
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
TOXBASE guidance is only as good as the risk assessment fed into it — a wrong agent or dose gives wrong advice.
Timed drug levels must be taken at the correct interval (e.g. paracetamol at 4h post-ingestion); too-early samples mislead.
Modified-release and staggered ingestions extend the window of risk and change monitoring — escalate to NPIS if uncertain.
🚩 Do NOT rely on gut decontamination or induced emesis routinely. Activated charcoal is only useful early and is contraindicated with a reduced or unprotected airway (aspiration risk). Ipecac-induced emesis is obsolete and dangerous. Always risk-assess and use TOXBASE/NPIS rather than guessing.
🎓 TOXBASE online FIRST, NPIS phone for complex or severe cases. Activated charcoal within ~1 hour if the airway is safe (not for alcohols, metals, lithium, hydrocarbons). Learn the antidote–toxin pairs cold — they are classic exam single-best-answers.
